prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
Before anything touches the network, the browser takes the address apart into scheme, host, port, path and query, and it uses the scheme to fill in port 443 when none is given. It then checks whether it has a reason not to go to the network at all: a service worker registered for the origin may answer the request itself, the HTTP cache may hold a fresh copy that needs no revalidation, and the browser's HSTS list, which includes a preloaded set shipped with the browser plus any hosts that previously sent a Strict-Transport-Security header, may force HTTPS even for a link typed as http. If the response is not available locally, the browser consults its proxy configuration, which can route the whole conversation through an intermediary, and then sets about finding where the host actually lives.

Name resolution comes first because TCP connects to IP addresses and not to names. The browser looks in its own DNS cache, then asks the operating system, which checks its cache and the hosts file before sending a query to the configured recursive resolver, often one run by the ISP, the router or a public provider, and increasingly reached over an encrypted channel such as DNS over HTTPS. If the resolver does not already hold the answer, it walks down the hierarchy: a root server points it to the servers for the top-level domain, those point it to the domain's authoritative nameservers, and the authoritative server returns the records, typically A for IPv4 and AAAA for IPv6, possibly after following a CNAME alias to another name such as a CDN hostname. Each record carries a time to live that tells every cache along the way how long it may be reused, which is why a warm lookup costs microseconds while a cold one can cost tens or hundreds of milliseconds, and why a DNS change takes time to be seen everywhere. Browsers may also ask for HTTPS records, which can announce that the server supports HTTP/3 and let the browser skip discovery.

With addresses in hand, the browser first looks for an existing connection to the same origin that it can reuse, since an idle HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection makes everything below unnecessary. When there is none, it picks an address, usually racing IPv6 against IPv4 with a small head start for IPv6 so that a broken path on one family does not stall the page, an approach known as Happy Eyeballs. Over TCP, the connection begins with a three-way handshake in which the client sends a SYN, the server replies with a SYN-ACK and the client acknowledges, which costs one full round trip before any application data can flow. Over QUIC, which carries HTTP/3 on top of UDP, the transport and cryptographic handshakes are merged, and the browser normally learns it may use QUIC from an Alt-Svc header seen on an earlier visit or from the DNS record, and otherwise starts with TCP.

On top of TCP, TLS then establishes an encrypted and authenticated channel. In TLS 1.3 the client sends a ClientHello naming the protocol versions and cipher suites it supports, a key share for a Diffie-Hellman exchange, the Server Name Indication extension carrying the hostname so that a server hosting many sites knows which certificate to present, and an ALPN list offering h2 and http/1.1 so that the HTTP version is agreed within the same exchange. The server answers with its own key share, which lets both sides derive the same session keys without ever transmitting them, and everything after that point is already encrypted, including the server's certificate chain and a signature over the handshake transcript proving that it holds the private key matching the certificate. The browser validates this by building a chain from the leaf certificate through intermediates to a root it trusts in the operating system or browser store, checking that the hostname matches one of the certificate's subject alternative names, that the dates are valid, that the certificate has not been revoked, which is usually established through a stapled OCSP response or a browser-maintained revocation list instead of a live query, and in Chrome and other browsers that the certificate comes with proof of inclusion in public certificate transparency logs. A failure at any of these steps produces the full-page certificate warning, and success ends with both sides sending Finished messages, so TLS 1.3 adds one round trip on top of TCP, while a returning client holding a session ticket can resume more cheaply and even send early data in its first flight, though that early data can be replayed by an attacker, which is why servers restrict it to requests that are safe to repeat.

Only now does the browser send the actual HTTP request, having waited through roughly two to three round trips, each as long as the physical distance and network allow, which is the main reason CDNs place servers near users. The request consists of a method and path, a Host header (or :authority in HTTP/2 and 3), and a set of headers the browser adds on its own, including User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Encoding listing the compression it can decode, Accept-Language, any cookies stored for the domain and path that apply, and cache validators such as If-None-Match when it holds a stale copy. In HTTP/2 and 3 these headers are compressed with HPACK or QPACK and sent in binary frames on a numbered stream, so many requests can share one connection, whereas HTTP/1.1 sends plain text and handles one request at a time per connection.

The request then arrives at whatever sits in front of the application: frequently a CDN edge, which may answer from cache and never touch the origin, or a load balancer that terminates TLS and forwards the request over a private network to a backend, where a web server or framework routes it to a handler that may query a database, call other services and render a response. The status line and headers are sent ahead of the body, and the moment the first byte of that response reaches the browser, which includes the trip back across the network plus whatever time the server spent computing, is what performance tools report as time to first byte. A slow TTFB can therefore come from any link in this chain, whether a cold DNS lookup, a distant server, a heavy certificate chain or slow application code, and the timing breakdown in the browser's network panel, which separates DNS lookup, initial connection, SSL and waiting, tells you which of these to look at first.
